title: The King's Indian chain: two wings, two breaks, one race
outcomes: Recognises the app's King's Indian chain in either orientation
Names each side's break and target: White's c4-c5 against d6, Black's ...f5 against e4
Checks the support for a break before starting it: counts what attacks and defends c5, and knows that a clear f6 only makes ...f5 legal, not ready
Finds moves in the structure without being told the plan

steps.text:
The app's **King's Indian chain**: pawns on c4, d5 and e4 against pawns on d6, e5 and g6 (colours may be reversed). This is the app's own definition.
The centre is locked, so each side attacks on its own wing. Rule of thumb: attack the base, not the head. White plays c4-c5 against d6, the base of Black's d6-e5 pair; Black plays ...f5 against e4.

steps.caption: White to move. The centre is locked, so each side attacks on its own wing. The pawn on b4 supports the break c5.

line.say: c5 attacks d6. If dxc5, bxc5 recaptures and the pawn on e5 loses its pawn support.
Black answers on the other wing: f5 attacks the pawn on e4.

claims.statement: After c5 the White pawn on c5 attacks d6, the base of Black's d6-e5 pair.
After c5 dxc5, one White pawn (on b4) can recapture on c5.
After c5 dxc5 bxc5, the pawn on e5 is no longer protected by a Black pawn.
At depth 16 the engine's best move is c5; c5 is within 0.4 pawns of it.
After c5 and f5, the Black pawn on f5 attacks e4.
The bishop on e3 attacks c5, so it backs the break.
The bishop on g7 attacks f6 and e5 but not d4: the pawn on e5 blocks it.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** A break needs support: count its attackers and defenders. Here c5 is backed by the pawn on b4 and the bishop on e3. ...f5 first needs f6 cleared (a knight there blocks the pawn), which makes it legal, not ready. Each break is a race on its own wing: check how fast theirs is first. The pawn on e5 also blocks the bishop on g7.

steps.title: Same break, one pawn different
steps.prompt: In the first two positions only a White b-pawn differs (on b4, or not yet there). Predict whether c5 works in each, then check. The third position is the worked example with one pawn moved: is it still the chain?

steps.text: **Counting the race.** Compare the two breaks. If yours is ready and theirs is not, starting yours is a candidate; if theirs is ready and yours is not, check whether you must slow theirs down first. Count moves, not hopes, and look for forcing moves that change the count. This is a rule of thumb. Next, unlabeled positions: start a break, prepare it, or wait?

steps.prompt: Think about the positions you played without hints. What was your break, and what supported it? Write one line.
